title: GDC registration & fitness to practise
blurb: Joining the register when you qualify, the annual renewal, indemnity, and what fitness to practise means, what triggers it and how the process works.
question: You've just passed your NEBDN Diploma. A friend who qualified last year tells you she forgot to renew her registration in July but is "still working while she sorts it out". What must you do to start working as a qualified dental nurse, and what should your friend be doing?

teach.body: The General Dental Council (GDC) regulates dental professionals across the UK, and its purpose is to protect the public. It keeps the register, sets the Standards for the Dental Team, quality-assures training and investigates concerns about registrants. "Dental nurse" is a protected title: working as one or calling yourself one while not registered is illegal. Trainees on a recognised training programme can work under supervision while they study, but once you qualify you must be registered before you work as a dental nurse.

teach.h: From trainee to registered dental nurse

items.label: Enrolled on a recognised programme
items.sub: Work under supervision as a trainee

items.label: Pass the Knowledge Test and Professional Discussion
Register with the GDC on eGDC
items.sub: Fee, health and character declarations, indemnity

items.label: You can work and use the title

teach.body: The registration year for dental care professionals runs from 1 August to 31 July. Every year you pay the annual retention fee and make declarations, including your CPD statement and confirmation that you have appropriate indemnity. If you don't renew, you are removed from the register and must stop working as a dental nurse straight away until you are restored. You must also tell the GDC if you face criminal proceedings or a finding by another regulator, and keep your details up to date.

items.label: registration year ends: renew before this

teach.caption: You are prompted for your CPD statement when you renew. The GDC accepts it up to 28 August, but only CPD done by 31 July counts for that year.

teach.body: By law, every registrant must have appropriate indemnity or insurance so that a patient who is harmed can be compensated. Many dental nurses are covered by their employer's arrangements, while others take out their own. Either way, it is your responsibility to check you are covered for everything you do, including additional skills such as taking radiographs or applying fluoride varnish. Working without cover puts your registration at risk.

Being fit to practise means having the skills, knowledge, character and health to practise safely and effectively. The GDC investigates when there is a concern that a registrant's fitness to practise may be impaired. The process is there to protect patients and public confidence, not to punish ordinary mistakes. A health condition is not a problem in itself if you manage it responsibly and it doesn't put patients at risk.

teach.h: What can trigger a fitness to practise case
head: Ground
Example
rows: Dishonesty, e.g. declaring CPD you didn't do; breaching confidentiality
Repeated unsafe infection control despite support
An untreated condition that affects safe practice
e.g. a finding by a nursing or medical regulator
teach.caption: Working while unregistered, without indemnity or outside your scope can also lead to action.

steps.sub: Patient, colleague, employer, police or self

steps.label: Initial assessment
steps.sub: Is it a fitness to practise matter?

steps.label: Case examiners
steps.sub: Close, advise, warn, agree undertakings or refer

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: No action, reprimand, conditions, suspension or erasure

teach.caption: If patients may be at risk while a case is investigated, an Interim Orders Committee can suspend or restrict registration in the meantime.

teach.body: GDC Principle 8 says you must raise concerns if patients are at risk, whether that's about a colleague's behaviour, performance or health, or your own. Usually you start with your practice's policy or manager. If that doesn't work, or the concern is serious, you can go to the GDC or another external body, and the law protects workers who raise concerns in the public interest. You are personally accountable for your actions to patients, the GDC, your team and the public, so be honest and cooperate with any investigation.

teach.text: A lapsed registration means you must STOP working as a dental nurse immediately until you're restored. "Working while you sort it out" is illegal practice.

items: The GDC protects the public; "dental nurse" is a protected title.
Register when you qualify; renew every year by 31 July with your fee, CPD statement and indemnity declaration.
Lapsed registration: stop practising until restored.
Indemnity is a legal requirement; check your cover includes everything you do.
FtP grounds: misconduct, deficient performance, adverse health, conviction or caution, another regulator's finding.
Process: concern, assessment, investigation, case examiners, hearing, outcome (up to erasure).

summary: You can now explain why the GDC register exists, describe how to register on qualifying and stay registered each year, explain the indemnity requirement, define fitness to practise, list what can trigger a case, outline the GDC process and its outcomes, and explain your duty to raise concerns.

A.q: A dental nurse is completing the annual GDC renewal. What must they confirm as part of it?
options: Their CPD and that they hold indemnity
Their appraisal scores and salary
The number of patients they've seen
That their employer is CQC-registered
A.why: The annual renewal includes a CPD statement and a declaration that the registrant has appropriate indemnity.

whyNot.1: Appraisal and pay are employment matters, not GDC declarations.
whyNot.2: The GDC doesn't ask for patient numbers.
whyNot.3: Practice registration with the CQC is the provider's responsibility, not part of your renewal.

A.q: A dental nurse's registration lapses because she forgot to renew. What must she do?
options: Keep working while she sorts it out
Stop practising until she is restored
Work only under a dentist's supervision
Carry on if she renews within a month
A.why: Without registration she cannot legally work as a dental nurse, so she must stop until she is restored to the register.

whyNot.0: Working while unregistered is illegal practice.
whyNot.2: Supervision doesn't make unregistered practice legal.
whyNot.3: There is no grace month for working while off the register.

A.q: Which of these is a recognised ground on which the GDC may find a registrant's fitness to practise impaired?
options: Being late for work on one occasion
Disagreeing professionally with a colleague
A criminal conviction or caution
Taking annual leave in August
A.why: A conviction or caution is one of the grounds for impaired fitness to practise.

whyNot.0: A one-off lateness is a workplace matter, not a regulatory one.
whyNot.1: Professional disagreement is normal and isn't a fitness to practise issue.
whyNot.3: Taking leave has nothing to do with fitness to practise.

B.q: What is the main purpose of the GDC's fitness to practise process?
options: To punish registrants for any error
To settle pay disputes with employers
To handle patient refunds for poor treatment
To protect patients and public confidence
B.why: Fitness to practise exists to protect patients and maintain public confidence in dental professionals.

whyNot.0: It isn't about punishing ordinary mistakes.
whyNot.2: Refunds are handled through complaints procedures, not fitness to practise.

B.q: Why must dental professionals have indemnity or insurance cover?
options: So patients can be compensated if harmed
So the practice can claim tax relief
So the GDC can reduce the annual fee
So that CPD courses are free of charge
B.why: Indemnity makes sure patients can receive compensation if they are harmed by a registrant's care.

whyNot.2: Indemnity doesn't affect the GDC's fee.
whyNot.3: Indemnity has nothing to do with CPD costs.

B.q: A dental nurse has just passed her NEBDN Diploma. What must happen before she works as a qualified dental nurse?
options: She must complete 50 hours of CPD
She must join the GDC register
She must be appraised by her employer
She must pass a CQC inspection
B.why: Qualified dental nurses must be on the GDC register before they work under the title.

whyNot.0: CPD starts with your first cycle after registration; it isn't a condition of joining.
whyNot.2: Appraisal is good practice, not a legal requirement to work.
whyNot.3: CQC inspects practices, not individual nurses.

C.q: Which of these is most likely to lead to a fitness to practise investigation?
options: Asking for training on a new sterilizer
Taking a sick day with flu
Declaring CPD hours that weren't done
Raising a concern about a colleague
C.why: A false CPD declaration is dishonesty, which is misconduct and can impair fitness to practise.

whyNot.0: Asking for training shows insight and is good practice.
whyNot.1: Short-term illness is not a fitness to practise matter.
whyNot.3: Raising concerns is a professional duty, and the law protects those who do.

C.q: After a GDC investigation, who decides whether a case should be closed or referred to a hearing?
options: The practice manager
The GDC case examiners
The Care Quality Commission
NEBDN's assessment panel
C.why: Case examiners review the evidence and decide whether to close the case, give advice or a warning, agree undertakings or refer it to a Practice Committee.

whyNot.0: Practice managers have no role in GDC decisions.
whyNot.2: The CQC regulates services, not individual registrants.
whyNot.3: NEBDN awards qualifications; it doesn't decide GDC cases.

C.q: Which is the most serious outcome a GDC Practice Committee can impose?
options: A formal reprimand
Conditions on practice
Suspension from the register
Erasure from the register
C.why: Erasure removes the registrant from the register, so they can no longer practise.

whyNot.0: A reprimand is the least serious sanction.
whyNot.1: Conditions restrict practice but allow the person to keep working.
whyNot.2: Suspension is temporary; erasure is more serious.

reteach.title: It's like a driving licence
reteach.question: You can't drive without passing your test, holding a licence and having insurance. How does that compare with working as a dental nurse?

blocks.body: Passing your driving test is like passing your NEBDN Diploma. Your licence is your GDC registration, and your car insurance is your indemnity. You keep the licence valid by renewing it, just as you renew your registration every year and keep up your CPD. Serious driving offences can lead to points or a ban; serious concerns about a registrant can lead to conditions, suspension or erasure. And if your licence has expired, you don't drive until it's renewed.

explain.body: Once you qualify, you apply to the GDC through eGDC, pay the fee and make declarations about your health, character and indemnity. Only registered people may work as, or call themselves, a dental nurse.

test.q: Who can legally call themselves a 'dental nurse'?
options: Anyone working in a dental practice
Only someone on the GDC register
Anyone with a first aid certificate
Any receptionist after six months
test.why: "Dental nurse" is a protected title; only GDC registrants can use it.

whyNot.0: Working in a practice doesn't give you the title.
whyNot.2: First aid training isn't a dental nursing qualification.
whyNot.3: Time in a non-clinical role doesn't lead to registration.

explain.body: The DCP registration year runs 1 August to 31 July. Renew by 31 July: pay the annual retention fee and make your CPD and indemnity declarations. Lapsed? Stop working until restored.

items.label: Renewal opens on eGDC
items.sub: About six weeks before year end

test.q: By what date must dental nurses renew their GDC registration each year?
options: 31 December
31 March
31 July
31 October
test.why: The registration year for dental care professionals ends on 31 July.

whyNot.0: 31 December is the end of the dentists' registration year.
whyNot.1: 31 March is the end of the financial year.
whyNot.3: 31 October has no link to GDC registration.

explain.body: Fitness to practise may be impaired by misconduct, deficient professional performance, adverse physical or mental health, a conviction or caution, or a finding by another regulator.

test.q: Which is NOT a ground on which fitness to practise may be impaired?
options: Misconduct
Adverse physical or mental health
Deficient professional performance
A patient changing practice
test.why: A patient choosing another practice is their right and says nothing about the registrant's fitness to practise.

whyNot.1: Adverse health is a recognised ground.
whyNot.2: Deficient professional performance is a recognised ground.

explain.body: If patients are at risk, you must raise concerns, first through your practice's policy or manager, then externally (for example the GDC) if nothing is done or it's serious. The law protects people who raise concerns.

test.q: A colleague often comes to work smelling of alcohol. You told the manager, but nothing has been done. What should you do?
options: Escalate it, for example to the GDC
Ignore it now you've told the manager
Confront them in front of patients
Post about it anonymously online
test.why: If an internal concern isn't acted on and patients may be at risk, you should escalate it externally.

whyNot.1: Your duty to protect patients continues if nothing changes.
whyNot.2: Public confrontation is unprofessional and unsafe.
whyNot.3: Social media is not an appropriate way to raise concerns.
